whole_public_config_unique_fields_in_ori.title: Five outgoing centers in a 16-realization cube move
whole_public_config_unique_fields_in_ori.description: One fixed algebraic crossed boundary admits an incoming exponent-16 realization and at least five distinct outgoing centers, exceeding the stated maximum-three expectation.
plain_language: A local cube move replaces one central point by another while keeping six boundary points fixed. The quadrilateral rule equates the sums of opposite side lengths raised to a chosen power.

At power 16, this note gives one fixed algebraic boundary with an incoming center and at least five outgoing choices. The same boundary works for all of them; its segments cross, so this is a realization allowing crossings.
result: Six fixed distinct algebraic points A₁,…,A₆, with both alternating triples noncollinear, admit an incoming center Z and at least five distinct outgoing centers X at α = 16. Every selected center differs from every boundary point.

A quadrilateral PQRS is an α-quad when |P−Q|^α + |R−S|^α = |P−S|^α + |Q−R|^α. The three incoming ordered faces are A₁A₂A₃Z, A₃A₄A₅Z and A₅A₆A₁Z; the three outgoing ordered faces are A₂A₃A₄X, A₄A₅A₆X and A₆A₁A₂X. All six identities hold for the same boundary.

The outgoing centers are at least five intersections of two distinct smooth construction curves sharing the focus A₂. This exceeds the at-most-three expectation for α > 1 in Melotti–Ramassamy–Thévenin, Remark 4.8, p. 811, and the maximum-three conjecture in the crossing-permitted workshop setting, p. 1785. The cited existence theorem is a separate statement.
why_it_works: Set A = (0,0), B = (2073/10000,0), C = (4719/10000,64/10000) and λ = 27/1250. The outgoing equations are |X−B|¹⁶ − |X−A|¹⁶ = λ and |X−C|¹⁶ − |X−A|¹⁶ = 1.

With s = |X−A|¹⁶, nonnegative real eighth roots give the three squared distances. An invertible linear system recovers X; one continuous residual G(s) then characterizes the original equations in both directions, retaining all real-branch constraints.

Strict rational signs at 9/10000, 11/10000, 13/10000, 1/2, 1 and 10¹⁶ alternate. The intermediate value theorem supplies a zero in each of five disjoint finite intervals. Different s give different centers; uniqueness within an interval is unnecessary. A concavity estimate controls the remote endpoint without subtracting nearly equal large radicals.

Three uniquely defined real roots of monotone rational polynomials fix the other boundary vertices. Their exact edge-power identities telescope. For this same fixed boundary, a second continuous residual has opposite strict endpoint signs and produces an actual incoming center. The written algebra verifies every incoming and outgoing ordered face, including the dependent third incoming identity.
Exact rational enclosures separate the selected centers from boundary vertices and every line through a boundary pair. A strict orientation pattern proves an interior crossing of [A₁,A₂] and [A₃,A₄].

Each common-focus curve is individually smooth because its powered-distance difference has a nonzero gradient. The boundary point A₃ lies on one curve and has a strictly positive residual for the other, proving that the two curves are distinct sets. This individual regularity does not assert joint transversality of their intersections.

The original standard-library verifier and rational certificate accompany the proof. Its default command recomputes and compares the complete certificate without writing; integer and Fraction arithmetic decide the signs. The existence argument uses the written distance equivalence, monotone boundary definitions, strict signs and exact face identities.
limitations: The fixed boundary crosses. It cannot yield a proper embedding for any choice of central point, and the construction concerns the realization and immersion conventions that permit crossings.

At least five is a lower bound. The exact total for this boundary and a universal maximum are undetermined here. No result for α < 1, root uniqueness within the brackets or joint intersection transversality is asserted.
The note does not establish historical firstness, independence from unknown work or the present worldwide status of stronger questions.
background: Melotti–Ramassamy–Thévenin define the α-quad and cube-move realization setting, including crossed faces. Their Remark 4.8 states the common-focus intersection-count expectation addressed by this construction. The Oberwolfach contribution states the corresponding maximum-three conjecture for crossing-permitted α-immersions.

Weighted-distance and pure-power families predate this note. Ash–Bolker study costs φ(|x−P|)+w(P), including a fourth-power example. Their separate oscillatory cost t+k sin(t) is a different example and does not itself settle this pure-power shared-focus count.

Bourne–Peletier–Roper define p-power costs |x−xᵢ|^p−wᵢ in the author manuscript, Definition 4.12; Bourne–Roper also discuss this established family. At p = 16 with weights (0,λ,1), equality of the three costs is exactly the displayed outgoing system. The contribution here is the explicit fixed-boundary count construction, with its incoming witness and face identities.

whole_public_config_unique_fields_in_ori.author: Alec Kriebel
whole_public_config_unique_fields_in_ori.abstract: We specify six algebraic boundary points, an incoming center, and at least five distinct outgoing centers for a cube move of 16-realizations. Existence follows from strict rational sign bounds for two continuous one-variable residuals. The boundary parameters are uniquely defined real roots of monotone polynomials. This contradicts the at-most-three expectation for construction curves sharing a focus in Remark 4.8 of Melotti–Ramassamy–Thévenin, in the realization setting allowing crossings. The fixed boundary is crossed, so the example concerns no proper embedding. Neither the exact number of centers for this boundary nor a universal maximum is determined.

whole_public_config_unique_fields_in_ori.title: Negative answers to the printed totally mixed face questions
whole_public_config_unique_fields_in_ori.description: Two lattice 5-polytopes refute Payne’s printed totally mixed face claims: a disconnected, nonshellable order complex with rational Betti numbers (2,22).
plain_language: A Minkowski sum adds every point of one polytope to every point of another. Each exposed face has canonical faces from the two summands. The printed question keeps only faces where both summands have positive dimension and their dimensions add exactly.

For two explicit lattice polytopes in five dimensions, the resulting face-inclusion complex splits into two loop-filled graphs. This gives negative answers to both the shellability and sphere-wedge homology assertions in the printed question.
result: Let D = conv(0,e₁,e₂,e₃,e₄) be the standard four-simplex and I = [0,1]. Both P₁ = D × I and P₂ = (−D) × I are full-dimensional lattice 5-polytopes.

Retain F = F₁ + F₂ when its canonical summands, exposed by the same functional, satisfy dim F₁ > 0, dim F₂ > 0 and dim F = dim F₁ + dim F₂. Form the ordinary order complex: its vertices are qualifying faces and its simplices are nonempty strict chains. No artificial minimum or maximum is adjoined.

This complex is K ⊔ K. Each K is a connected pure graph with 50 vertices and 60 edges, homotopy equivalent to a wedge of eleven circles. The ordinary rational homology is H₀ = ℚ², H₁ = ℚ²² and Hⱼ = 0 for j ≥ 2. The complex is not shellable under either pure or standard nonpure shellability, and it does not have the homology of a wedge of three-spheres.
why_it_works: Proper nonempty faces of the simplex difference D−D are indexed by nonempty disjoint subsets A,B of its five vertex labels. Their dimensions add, and inclusion is exactly containment in each label set. The positive-dimension filter keeps the size pairs (2,2), (2,3) and (3,2): 30 minimal faces and 20 maximal faces, with 60 comparabilities and no three-element strict chains. Their graph K is connected.

The common interval factor is decisive. Qualifying faces with a nonzero interval coefficient in their exposing functional form the two endpoint copies of K. With zero coefficient, each summand gains an interval direction but the sum gains only one, so exact dimension additivity fails. The full-base end faces and the whole sum fail the filter too; no qualifying face links the two copies.

Each connected graph has 60−50+1 = 11 independent cycles. In any proposed shelling, the first edge from the second component meets the earlier edges only in the empty face, rather than the required zero-dimensional intersection. This rules out both shellability conventions. Two components and nonzero first homology also rule out the printed sphere-wedge target.
The paper gives the complete analytic face argument. Two exact standard-library checkers accompany it as supplementary verification; the proof does not depend on running them.
definitions_and_limits: The shared interval deliberately makes this example nongeneric. Payne’s printed Problem 3 states no general-position condition. No generic-perturbation theorem, minimum-dimension claim, historical firstness or present worldwide openness is asserted.

The exact-additivity filter is different from Adiprasito’s public 2020 manuscript underlying a 2024 article, which requires dim(Σ_{i∈J} Fᵢ) ≥ |J| for every nonempty index subset J. A vertical face with summand dimensions 2 and 2 and sum dimension 3 passes those lower bounds but fails exact additivity. This note does not contradict that stable-intersection theorem or settle its shellability question.

Adiprasito and coauthors’ colorful-Gale “totally mixed” convention instead requires facets of the summands. Hiatt–Simpson–Wang–Wu v2, Section 8, concerns a different Schön subvariety of (ℂ*)⁸ and its tropical link; no identification with this two-summand face poset is supplied.
background: Canonical Minkowski face decomposition and simplex-difference geometry are classical. Fukuda–Weibel provide the general decomposition statement, and Sturmfels–Tevelev’s scaled opposite tetrahedra give the earlier six-point homology control. That zero-dimensional complex is shellable, so it does not by itself prove nonshellability. The common-interval construction supplies the positive-dimensional disconnected example here.

whole_public_config_unique_fields_in_ori.author: Alec Kriebel
whole_public_config_unique_fields_in_ori.abstract: For two polytopes, retain the faces of their Minkowski sum whose two canonical summands have positive dimensions and whose dimension is the sum of those dimensions. This is the definition in Payne’s printed Oberwolfach question. Let D be the standard four-simplex and I = [0,1]. For the full-dimensional lattice polytopes D × I and (−D) × I in ℝ⁵, the qualifying-face order complex is a disjoint union of two connected pure graphs, each with 50 vertices and 60 edges. Its rational Betti numbers are (2,22,0,…). Thus both printed assertions, shellability and the homology of a wedge of three-spheres, fail. The shared interval factor deliberately produces a nongeneric example. The argument concerns the printed additive-dimension definition; it does not settle shellability for the different mixed faces used in stable tropical intersections.
